explanations.explanation: David says it plainly: “I will show kindness to Hanun son of Nahash, because his father showed kindness to me.” Nahash was the king of the Ammonites who just died, and Hanun is his son. David is paying kindness back with kindness. That's a man who remembers who was good to him.

explanations.answer: Hanun once helped David in battle
explanations.explanation: Hanun has only just become king, so nothing in the text says he did anything for David yet. The reason David gives is about Hanun's father, Nahash, king of the Ammonites. David says, “…because his father showed kindness to me.” So the kindness David names belongs to Nahash, not Hanun.

explanations.answer: Hanun sent David a gift of silver
explanations.explanation: No gift shows up here, friend. David reaches out first, and his reason is Nahash, the late king of the Ammonites: “…because his father showed kindness to me.” The silver in this story comes later, and it goes somewhere you wouldn't expect. This opening is just David being generous.

explanations.answer: Spy out the land and overthrow it
explanations.explanation: The princes of the Ammonites ask Hanun, “Have not his servants come to you to explore the land, spy it out, and overthrow it?” David sent comforters, and the princes called them spies. Hanun is the new king, and he has some very loud voices in his ear. Friend, I've seen a recipe get doubted less.

explanations.answer: Steal the royal treasure for David
explanations.explanation: Treasure never comes up in what the princes say. They say David's servants came to “…explore the land, spy it out, and overthrow it?” That's about exploring, spying and overthrowing, not grabbing valuables. It's a big accusation to make about men who came to console.

explanations.answer: Take Hanun back as a prisoner
explanations.explanation: The princes say nothing about taking Hanun anywhere. Their words to him are, “Have not his servants come to you to explore the land, spy it out, and overthrow it?” Their question is about the land and overthrowing it. Hanun, the new king, is the one they say it to.

The text says the opposite. Hanun took David's servants, shaved their beards, cut off their garments at the hips, and sent them away. David sent these men to console him, and that's how they were sent home. Honor was nowhere in that exchange.

Right, it's False. Hanun, the new king of the Ammonites, shaved their beards, cut off their garments at the hips, and sent them away. David's men came to console him and left humiliated. That one's a heavy moment, and I think it stings to read.

When someone told David what happened, he sent messengers to meet his men. The text says the men had been thoroughly humiliated. David told them, “Stay in Jericho until your beards have grown back, and then return.” He didn't send them back to Hanun.
No letter appears in this passage. David's first move is toward his own men: he sent messengers to meet them. The text says the men had been thoroughly humiliated. His attention goes to them first.

David does nothing of the sort, friend. He sends messengers to meet his men, and he tells them to stay in Jericho. They're not going back to Hanun's court. The text says the men had been thoroughly humiliated, and David looks after them.

explanations.answer: Until their beards have grown back
explanations.explanation: David tells them, “Stay in Jericho until your beards have grown back, and then return.” Jericho is a city, and that's where they wait. Beards grow on their own schedule. I'd know, since my mustache does what it wants.

explanations.answer: Until a full year has passed
explanations.explanation: David never names a length of time. He gives a condition: “Stay in Jericho until your beards have grown back, and then return.” It's the beards that set the clock, not the calendar. Nobody can rush a beard, friend.

explanations.answer: Until their new garments are ready
explanations.explanation: Garments were cut off at the hips, so you'd expect the fix to be clothes. But David's words are about the beards: “Stay in Jericho until your beards have grown back, and then return.” That's the wait. Jericho is where they stay while it happens.

They sent a thousand talents of silver to hire chariots and horsemen from Aram-naharaim, Aram-maacah, and Zobah. Those are Aramean regions. This came after the Ammonites realized they had become a stench to David. That's a lot of silver spent on hired soldiers.

explanations.answer: A peace gift for King David
explanations.explanation: The silver doesn't go to David at all. It goes to hire chariots and horsemen from Aram-naharaim, Aram-maacah, and Zobah. These are Aramean lands. The Ammonites were gearing up for a fight, not smoothing things over.

No walls are mentioned. The Ammonites spent the silver to hire chariots and horsemen from Aram-naharaim, Aram-maacah, and Zobah. They paid for other people's armies to come stand beside them. That's a thousand talents of silver, and not one brick.
It's True. David heard about it and sent Joab, his army commander, with the entire army of mighty men. David didn't send a small group. He sent the entire army of mighty men.
It's actually True. On hearing about the hired army, David sent Joab, his army commander, and the entire army of mighty men. David answered a big army with a big army. No halfway measures here.

explanations.answer: He splits his troops into two groups
explanations.explanation: Joab saw the battle lines before him and behind him. So he selected some of the best men of Israel to face the Arameans, and the rest went under his brother Abishai against the Ammonites. Two fronts, two groups. Joab, David's army commander, split his troops to meet both.

explanations.answer: He orders his troops to retreat
explanations.explanation: There's no retreat order anywhere. Joab, David's army commander, saw battle lines before him and behind him, and he divided his troops. Some went against the Arameans, and the rest went with his brother Abishai against the Ammonites. He turned around and faced both.

explanations.answer: He waits for David to come help
explanations.explanation: Joab doesn't wait for David here. The text says David sent Joab with the army, and then Joab arranges his troops. He picks some of the best men of Israel for the Arameans and puts the rest under his brother Abishai against the Ammonites. Nothing in the text has him waiting for help from David.

It's True. Joab, David's army commander, selected some of the best men of Israel and arrayed them against the Arameans. The rest went to his brother Abishai against the Ammonites. So Joab's group was the one set against the Arameans.

It's actually True. Joab selected some of the best men of Israel and arrayed them against the Arameans. Abishai, Joab's brother, led the rest against the Ammonites. Joab's group went where the hired army was.

explanations.answer: If one side is losing the other comes to help
explanations.explanation: Joab tells his brother Abishai that if the Arameans are too strong for him, Abishai will come to his rescue. And if the Ammonites are too strong for Abishai, Joab will come to his. Each brother covers the other. Two armies, one deal, and whoever gets pressed has help coming.

explanations.answer: If one side is losing both fall back to Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Falling back isn't in his plan. Joab says, “If the Arameans are too strong for me, then you will come to my rescue.” Abishai, his brother, is told the same thing in reverse. They promise to help each other, not leave.

explanations.answer: Whichever side wins first gets all the plunder
explanations.explanation: No plunder deal is made here. Joab tells Abishai, his brother, “And if the Ammonites are too strong for you, then I will come to your rescue.” He had the same promise for himself too. It's all about rescue, not about who gets what.

explanations.answer: He leaves the outcome to the LORD
explanations.explanation: Joab ends with, “May the LORD do what is good in His sight.” Right before that he says, “Be strong and let us fight bravely for our people and for the cities of our God.” He gives it everything he has and leaves the result with the LORD. That's a solid way to head into a fight.

explanations.answer: He promises the troops the plunder
explanations.explanation: Joab doesn't mention plunder. He says, “Be strong and let us fight bravely for our people and for the cities of our God. May the LORD do what is good in His sight.” His last words hand the outcome to the LORD. No prizes offered.

explanations.answer: He warns the troops not to run
explanations.explanation: There's no warning in his words. Joab says, “Be strong and let us fight bravely for our people and for the cities of our God.” He closes with “May the LORD do what is good in His sight.” It's encouragement, and then he trusts the LORD with the rest.

Joab and his troops advanced to fight the Arameans, and the Arameans fled before him. These were the chariots and horsemen the Ammonites hired with their silver. I've seen cookies leave a plate slower.
Nobody gets pushed back. Joab and his troops advance, and the Arameans flee before him. That's the army the Ammonites hired. The text has Joab moving forward.

Joab's men weren't trapped. They advanced, and the Arameans fled before him. Earlier, Joab told Abishai to come to his rescue if the Arameans were too strong for him. This time the text says the Arameans fled.

It's True. When the Ammonites saw that the Arameans had fled, they too fled before Abishai, Joab's brother, and they entered the city. The Ammonites had hired the Arameans, and once the hired help ran, they did too. After that, Joab went back to Jerusalem.
It's actually True. The Ammonites saw the Arameans flee, and they too fled before Joab's brother Abishai. They went into their city. They didn't hold their ground.

It's True. When the report reached David, he gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan, and advanced toward the Arameans. That's the king leading himself, not just sending a commander. Shophach, the commander of Hadadezer's army, was leading the other side.
It's actually True. David gathered all Israel and crossed the Jordan. He advanced toward the Arameans and arrayed for battle. This time David himself gathered Israel and went.

explanations.answer: The Arameans flee and Shophach is killed
explanations.explanation: The Arameans fled before Israel. David killed seven thousand of their charioteers and forty thousand foot soldiers. He also killed Shophach, the commander of their army. The Arameans had come with a lot, and it didn't hold.

explanations.answer: The Arameans win and David pulls back
explanations.explanation: David doesn't pull back. The Arameans fled before Israel, and David killed seven thousand charioteers and forty thousand foot soldiers. Shophach, the commander of their army, was killed too. David won this one.

explanations.answer: Both armies pull back with no winner
explanations.explanation: This one has a clear winner. The Arameans fled before Israel. David killed seven thousand of their charioteers and forty thousand foot soldiers, and he killed Shophach, their commander. The text says the Arameans fled, so there's no draw here.

explanations.answer: Make peace with David and serve him
explanations.explanation: Hadadezer's subjects saw that Israel had beaten them. So they made peace with David and became subject to him. They chose peace.

explanations.answer: Ask the Ammonites for more silver
explanations.explanation: Nobody asks for more silver. After Hadadezer's subjects saw they'd been defeated by Israel, they made peace with David and became subject to him. The text then says the Arameans were unwilling to help the Ammonites anymore.

explanations.answer: Pull back and plan another attack
explanations.explanation: No second attack is mentioned. Hadadezer's subjects saw they'd been defeated by Israel, and they made peace with David. They became subject to him. Peace is what the text gives them.

The text says the opposite. Hadadezer's subjects made peace with David and became subject to him, and the Arameans were unwilling to help the Ammonites anymore. The Ammonites had paid a thousand talents of silver to hire Arameans. Now those Arameans were unwilling to help them.

Right, it's False. Hadadezer's subjects made peace with David and became subject to him, and the Arameans were unwilling to help the Ammonites anymore. The Ammonites had paid a thousand talents of silver to hire Arameans. And now the Arameans wouldn't help.
The text says otherwise. Joab led out the army and ravaged the land of the Ammonites, but David remained in Jerusalem. Joab, David's army commander, did the marching. David stayed in Jerusalem.
Right, it's False. Joab led out the army, and David remained in Jerusalem. Joab ravaged the land of the Ammonites and came to Rabbah. David was not on the road with them.

explanations.answer: Joab attacks Rabbah and demolishes it
explanations.explanation: Joab came to Rabbah, an Ammonite city, and besieged it. Then he attacked Rabbah and demolished it. He started a siege and finished the job.

explanations.answer: Joab gives up and heads back home
explanations.explanation: Joab doesn't give up. He besieged Rabbah, an Ammonite city, and then attacked and demolished it. The siege ended with the city down.

explanations.answer: Rabbah holds out and Joab moves on
explanations.explanation: Rabbah doesn't hold out. Joab besieged it, then attacked Rabbah and demolished it. He didn't move on until the job was done.

The crown was found to weigh a talent of gold, and it was set with precious stones. A talent is a big weight, and this was a whole talent of gold. My chef's hat is made of cloth and weighs next to nothing.
Silver was what the Ammonites spent on hired chariots earlier in the story. The crown is different. It was found to weigh a talent of gold, and it was set with precious stones.
Bronze isn't in this verse. The crown was found to weigh a talent of gold, and it was set with precious stones. Gold and jewels, friend. Nobody's calling that a bronze-medal crown.
David took the crown from the head of the Ammonite king, and it was placed on David's head. It moved from one head to the other. That's a talent of gold changing heads.
It doesn't go back to their king. David took the crown from the head of their king, and it was placed on David's head. This verse doesn't hand it back to the Ammonite king.

The text says nothing about locking it away. David took the crown from their king's head, and it was placed on David's head. I know a thing or two about being shut away in a junk drawer, but this crown went on a head instead.
It's True. David brought out the people who were there and put them to work with saws, iron picks, and axes. The text says he did the same to all the Ammonite cities. It's a heavy part of the story.

It's actually True. David put the people to work with saws, iron picks, and axes, and he did the same to all the Ammonite cities. It wasn't just Rabbah. Then David and all his troops returned to Jerusalem.
